content.paragraph: In this section we use trigonometric identities to integrate certain combinations of trigonometric functions.

subsection.title: Integrals of Powers of Sine and Cosine
subsection.paragraph: We begin by considering integrals in which the integrand is a power of sine, a power of cosine, or a product of these.

problem.paragraph: Evaluate $$\int\cos^{3}xdx$$ .

Solution Simply substituting $$u = \cos x$$ isn’t helpful, since then $$du = - \sin xdx$$ . In order to integrate powers of cosine, we would need an extra $$\sin x$$ factor. Thus here we can separate one cosine factor and convert the remaining $$\cos^{2}x$$ factor to an expression involving sine using the identity $$\sin^{2}x + \cos^{2}x = 1$$ :

The identity $$\sin^{2}x + \cos^{2}x = 1$$ enables us to convert back and forth between even powers of sine and cosine.

subsection.title: Integrals of Powers of Secant and Tangent
subsection.paragraph: We use similar reasoning to evaluate integrals of the form $${\int{\tan^{m}x}}\sec^{n}xdx$$ . Because $$({d \slash dx})\tan x = \sec^{2}x$$ , we can separate a $$\sec^{2}x$$ factor and convert the remaining (even) power of secant to an expression involving tangent using the identity $$\sec^{2}x = 1 + \tan^{2}x$$ . Or, since $$\left( {d \slash dx} \right)\sec x = \sec x\tan x$$ , we can separate a $$\sec x\tan x$$ factor and convert the remaining (even) power of tangent to secant.

problem.paragraph: Evaluate $${\int{\tan^{6}x}}\sec^{4}xdx$$ .

Solution If we separate one $$\sec^{2}x$$ factor, we can express the remaining $$\sec^{2}x$$ factor in terms of tangent using the identity $$\sec^{2}x = 1 + \tan^{2}x$$ . We can then evaluate the integral by substituting $$u = \tan x$$ so that $$du = \sec^{2}xdx$$ :
Find $${\int{\tan^{5}\theta}}\sec^{7}\theta d\theta$$ .

Solution If we separate a $$\sec^{2}\theta$$ factor, as in the preceding example, we are left with a $$\sec^{5}\theta$$ factor, which isn’t easily converted to tangent. However, if we separate a $$\sec\theta\tan\theta$$ factor, we can convert the remaining power of tangent to an expression involving only secant using the identity $$\tan^{2}\theta = \sec^{2}\theta - 1$$ . We can then evaluate the integral by substituting $$u = \sec\theta$$ , so $$du = \sec\theta\tan\theta d\theta$$ :

paragraph.math: $$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int{\tan^{5}}}\theta\sec^{7}\theta d\theta} = {{\int{\tan^{4}}}\theta\sec^{6}\theta\sec\theta\tan\theta d\theta}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\tan^{5}}}\theta\sec^{7}\theta d\theta} = {{\int{{({\sec^{2}\theta - 1})}^{2}}}\sec^{6}\theta\sec\theta\tan\theta d\theta}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\tan^{5}}}\theta\sec^{7}\theta d\theta} = {{\int{{({u^{2} - 1})}^{2}}}u^{6}du}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\tan^{5}}}\theta\sec^{7}\theta d\theta} = {\int{({u^{10} - 2u^{8} + u^{6}})}}du} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\tan^{5}}}\theta\sec^{7}\theta d\theta} = {\frac{u^{11}}{11} - 2\frac{u^{9}}{9} + \frac{u^{7}}{7} + C}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\tan^{5}}}\theta\sec^{7}\theta d\theta} = {\frac{1}{11}\sec^{11}\theta - \frac{2}{9}\sec^{9}\theta + \frac{1}{7}\sec^{7}\theta + C}} \end{array}$$
